results.verified_title: OECD Main Science and Technology Indicators: China’s sustained R&D-intensity catch-up
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the OECD Main Science and Technology Indicators (MSTI) dataset landing page, explicitly identified as the OECD international R&D database. Its release-cycle section links the 31 March 2026 OECD statistical briefing derived from that same database; 2026-03-31 denotes that documented March release, not a fabricated publication day for the undated landing page.
results.evidence_location: OECD MSTI landing page: “MSTI release cycle and highlights”; accompanying 31 March 2026 OECD MSTI statistical release, section “R&D intensity in the OECD area remains unchanged, China catches up”. Chinese National Bureau of Statistics, 16 October 2026 communiqué, section I.
results.specific_finding: China’s reported R&D intensity reached approximately 2.7% of GDP in 2024, matching the OECD-area average and exceeding the EU’s roughly 2.1%; Chinese national data subsequently report 2.80% in 2025, with basic research accounting for 7.21% of R&D expenditure. This is a sustained change in research-system scale and mix, not a claim that China leads in all research quality or commercial outcomes.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The OECD MSTI database is a continuing statistical series and its 31 March 2026 release explicitly states that China had caught up with OECD-area R&D intensity in 2024, ahead of the EU ratio. China’s statistical agency separately publishes 2024 intensity of 2.69% and 2025 intensity of 2.80%, plus a 13.3% year-on-year increase in 2025 basic-research expenditure. The figures are internally consistent as a trajectory but have different reference years.
results.corroboration_assessment: The Chinese statistical communiqué on a different domain substantiates the 2024–25 intensity direction and breakdown; WIPO independently describes China’s broader innovation-output position using a different indicator system. OECD comparisons still rely partly on Chinese national returns and are not a field audit of claimed performance.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: An increasing share of national resources devoted to R&D, together with rising basic-research spending, changes the scale and composition of China’s research ecosystem. This merits comparison of talent pipelines, research quality, collaboration opportunities and strategic dependencies against European funding trends.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar entry was supplied for this source. This extends an EU-centred perspective by juxtaposing 2024 EU R&D intensity around 2.1% with the Chinese 2024 OECD estimate and later 2025 national reporting; topical overlap elsewhere in the archive cannot be ruled out.
results.method_and_limitations: OECD comparisons use reported national statistics and revised definitions; 2025 Chinese numbers are official self-reports, not independently audited outcomes. GDP denominators, preliminary releases and inflation adjustments matter; reported spending does not demonstrate research productivity or quality.
results.reviewer_notes: The assigned OECD page is a dataset portal, not a dated China article. The dated OECD MSTI March 2026 companion report is essential for interpretation: https://www.oecd.org/en/data/insights/statistical-releases/2026/03/oecd-overall-rd-growth-stable-government-rd-budgets-decline-and-reorient-towards-defence.html . Distinct from candidate 10, which tests international scale/PPP, not the funding-share trajectory.

results.verified_title: United Kingdom: persistent high innovation rank supported by a concentrated university spin-out system
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the original WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 edition page, which links the sixth-ranked United Kingdom and the full official 2026 results. WIPO announced the edition on 29 September 2026. The linked WIPO narrative and independent UK digital-technology statistics were read for structural evidence.
results.source_type: international innovation indicator / national ecosystem analysis
results.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 home page ranking, #6 United Kingdom; accompanying GII 2026 results, ranking/innovation-cluster discussion. UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology 2026 Digital and Technologies Sector Statistics, section 5 “University Spinouts”.
results.specific_finding: The UK retained sixth place in WIPO’s 2026 innovation ranking. UK government statistics identify 655 digital-and-technology university spin-outs as of April 2026, including 518 in frontier technologies; these are concentrated at a small number of universities. This is an established structural route from university research to enterprise, rather than a claim that a new rank breakthrough occurred.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO’s 29 September 2026 index places the UK sixth, unchanged from 2025, and identifies prominent UK innovation clusters. UK official business-linked estimates separately count 655 university spin-outs in digital and technology, with 518 in frontier technology; Oxford and Cambridge alone account for a substantial share. A 2026 independent UKRI-commissioned review documents financing and regional concentration constraints.
results.corroboration_assessment: Government spin-out counts draw on HESA company-level data, rather than the WIPO composite-rank calculation; the independently authored UKRI review describes real translation and funding bottlenecks. Both are independent publishers and provide complementary, not identical, outcome measures.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: University IP, spin-out formation, research funding and investor links form a powerful but geographically concentrated research-commercialisation pathway. Studying its bottlenecks and measured spin-out population offers an alternative institutional comparison for European knowledge-transfer policy.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact assigned UK WIPO entry was identified in the supplied Radar links. The UK evidence supplies a non-EU comparison with European university commercialisation, without implying EU countries lack spin-out programmes or that the index rank proves policy superiority.
results.method_and_limitations: The GII is a composite index affected by normalization, changing indicators and reporting lags. The 655 figure covers UK digital/technology firms only, not all university spin-outs; business classifications and attribution to university research introduce measurement uncertainty. The UKRI review documents remaining finance gaps.
results.reviewer_notes: WIPO source is a 2026 international ranking, not a detailed UK-specific impact evaluation. Structural finding is justified by separately measured UK spinout statistics, with no claim of causality from rank to spinouts.

results.verified_title: Brazil: sustained innovation overperformance alongside renewed research funding, but concentrated capabilities
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the WIPO GII 2026 primary edition and the official WIPO detailed 2026 results covering Brazil’s #53 ranking and six-year overperformance. WIPO published the edition on 29 September 2026. A separate FAPESP research-policy data article reporting MCTI budget changes was also checked.
results.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 results, “Which economies do more with less?” and “Latin America and the Caribbean”, including Brazil’s #53 and sixth consecutive overperformer status. Revista Pesquisa FAPESP April 2025 “MCTI spending increased significantly between 2020 and 2024”.
results.specific_finding: Brazil ranked 53rd globally and second in Latin America in the 2026 GII; WIPO says it has exceeded the innovation performance expected for its income level for six consecutive years. Independent Brazilian research-policy data document a more than twofold real increase in committed MCTI funding between 2020 and 2024, while WIPO flags concentrated capacities and weak diffusion beyond major hubs.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO identifies Brazil as the only Latin American innovation overperformer for six consecutive years and points to its scientific base, trademarks, venture capital and São Paulo research cluster. Revista Pesquisa FAPESP documents MCTI committed budget from R$3.4bn in 2020 to R$8.7bn in 2024, with real-terms growth above 100%, largely through stronger FNDCT execution. These are different indicators and should not be collapsed into a single proven causal effect.
results.corroboration_assessment: Pesquisa FAPESP uses Brazilian public-budget records and reports a dated funding recovery, independently of WIPO’s composite innovation score. This supports a real policy-investment trend but does not prove the budget recovery caused the GII position or broad productivity improvements.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Brazil illustrates an innovation system with a large science base, focused intellectual-property and venture strengths and recovered public R&D funding, but substantial regional concentration and commercialization weaknesses. Those differences can expose options and blind spots in EU-centric global innovation comparisons.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact matching main Radar link was supplied for the Brazil country profile. The evidence adds Latin American investment and innovation-system structure to a primarily European monitoring frame; the main archive may still contain overlapping Brazilian developments.
results.method_and_limitations: GII ranks are relative to 138 other economies and fluctuate with methods and data availability; “overperformance” is model-relative and not a claim of globally high innovation intensity. Budget commitments are not direct realized R&D outcomes, and region-wide effects cannot be inferred from São Paulo.
results.reviewer_notes: Distinct from a headline-only innovation-rank story: retain the multiyear overperformance and independently documented research-budget trajectory; do not claim commercial impact is already proven.

results.verified_title: South Africa: repeated innovation overperformance despite declining real R&D spending
results.source_identity_basis: Opened WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 original edition, dated 29 September 2026, and its detailed country results naming South Africa as #63 and a ninth-year overperformer. Opened South Africa’s Department of Science, Technology and Innovation 29 October 2026 survey announcement and separate independent coverage.
results.source_type: international innovation benchmarking with national R&D survey comparison
results.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 detailed results, “Which economies do more with less?” (ninth consecutive overperformer) and Sub-Saharan Africa. South African DSTI “Real R&D spending declines as business investment weakens”, 29 October 2026, first paragraphs and business-sector section.
results.specific_finding: South Africa was ranked 63rd globally in WIPO’s 2026 GII and identified as an innovation overperformer for a ninth consecutive year. Yet its 2024/25 national R&D survey reports a 1.9% real decline in R&D expenditure and an R&D-intensity fall from 0.62% to 0.60% of GDP, with weaker business investment. The combination suggests sustained innovation strengths operating under deteriorating research-investment conditions.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO’s multiyear composite benchmarking places South Africa among lower-income relative innovation overperformers. Its national science department separately reports 2024/25 GERD of R44.237bn in nominal terms, declining 1.9% after inflation and lower GERD/GDP intensity; the fall is concentrated in the business sector. These measurements describe different aspects of the system and are not intrinsically contradictory.
results.corroboration_assessment: The independently conducted South African National R&D Survey supplies financial data distinct from WIPO’s composite score; sectoral press coverage checks its reported values but relies on the same underlying survey. The two independent indicator systems support a nuanced structural insight, not a claim of independently audited WIPO rankings.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A research system can remain productive relative to its income level while its business R&D base weakens in real terms. The contrast is consequential for innovation resilience, knowledge-transfer financing and international research partnerships involving South Africa.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact linked Radar entry was provided for South Africa’s WIPO profile. This adds evidence about African innovation strengths and financing constraints that can otherwise be missed by a Europe-first source selection.
results.method_and_limitations: Different reference periods: WIPO GII 2026 uses multiyear input data, while the latest South African survey reports financial year 2024/25. WIPO overperformance is relative to income and composite-method assumptions. Survey values are estimates; funding decline alone does not show reduced scientific output.
results.reviewer_notes: October 2026 South African survey is later than WIPO’s September release and is used as subsequent corroborating context, not to re-date the WIPO primary item.

results.verified_title: Singapore: world-leading innovation inputs and a long-horizon mission-oriented research strategy
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the original WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 edition page released 29 September 2026 and full WIPO results for Singapore. Opened Singapore National Research Foundation’s RIE2025/RIE2030 official programme description and Statistics Singapore’s independently tabulated annual R&D series.
results.source_type: international innovation-system benchmarking / government programme statistics
results.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 detailed results: Singapore ranks fifth overall, first for innovation inputs and ninth for outputs. NRF RIE overview, “RIE2030 Plan”; SingStat Research & Development latest series, 2022–2023 realized expenditure and R&D manpower.
results.specific_finding: Singapore held fifth place in WIPO’s 2026 GII, ranking first for innovation inputs but ninth for innovation outputs. Its government maintains an explicit multiyear research–enterprise policy architecture through RIE2030, while Singapore’s statistical office reports 2023 R&D spending of S$13.75bn (2.03% of GDP, versus 1.81% previously). The combination shows a high-capacity, deliberately coordinated innovation ecosystem with measurable conversion challenges.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO evaluates Singapore as a leading innovation-input system with a smaller but still high output ranking, indicating a gap between resource/environment advantages and output position. NRF’s RIE2030 programme identifies mission-driven Flagships and Grand Challenges, and realized historical investment is documented in SingStat annual R&D survey figures; these are genuine system characteristics, not proof of future policy success.
results.corroboration_assessment: National programme documents establish actual institutional architecture and intent, while SingStat’s annual R&D statistics document real expenditure distinct from WIPO ranking calculations. Neither proves that RIE2030 objectives will be achieved; the WIPO output/input gap remains an index-based diagnostic.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Singapore combines persistent high research investment, coordinated government priorities, translational programmes and targeted missions. Its measured input/output relationship provides a valuable non-EU contrast for governance, commercialization and allocation of research resources.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The package contains no exact matching Singapore main-Radar entry; this adds comparative evidence on a mature Asian innovation-governance model and innovation-output conversion, without presuming transferability to EU scale or institutions.
results.method_and_limitations: WIPO input/output rankings are composite, not a causal efficiency measure. RIE2030 commitments are programme plans, not realized outcomes; the available SingStat expenditure time series ends in 2023, so it does not establish 2026 spend or policy impact.
results.reviewer_notes: WIPO findings are about structural strengths and conversion constraints rather than a new 2026 research breakthrough.

results.verified_title: OECD March 2026: China approaches US R&D expenditure at PPP, but parity is benchmark-sensitive
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the exact assigned OECD statistical release, issued 31 March 2026, titled “OECD overall R&D growth stable; government R&D budgets decline and reorient towards defence”. The R&D comparisons and caveats come directly from this dated OECD analysis of Main Science and Technology Indicators.
results.evidence_location: OECD 31 March 2026 release, sections “The United States and China reach the one-trillion-dollar R&D milestone in 2024”; “Understanding international comparisons ... purchasing power”; “R&D intensity ... China catches up”.
results.specific_finding: OECD estimates for 2024 indicate Chinese R&D expenditure was about 102% of US expenditure under the OECD’s contemporaneous purchasing-power conversion, but closer to 90–95% using a fixed 2020 PPP benchmark and about 50% at market exchange rates. China and the US are extraordinarily large research investors, yet asserting an unqualified Chinese R&D lead would overstate what the statistics show.
results.primary_evidence_summary: OECD estimates China’s 2024 GERD at roughly USD 0.86tr in 2020 PPP-adjusted dollars, marginally above the US under the OECD 2024 PPP ratio; both reach approximately USD 1tr when expressed in 2024 prices. The same OECD source explicitly demonstrates how different purchasing-power and exchange-rate conventions materially change the relative ranking.
results.corroboration_assessment: China’s 2024 national statistics independently publish the underlying RMB expenditure and R&D/GDP intensity; WIPO’s 2026 assessment uses a separate innovation-indicator methodology and reports China’s scale of research and technology clusters. However OECD’s Chinese monetary input relies on national reporting, so national figures and OECD conversions are not two independent audits.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: The sheer scale of Chinese research financing affects global equipment demand, scientific workforce competition, publication and patent ecosystems, industrial supply chains and collaborative opportunities. Exact PPP methods are crucial for realistic comparisons against US and EU technological capacity.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact corresponding main Radar link was supplied. This adds a global scale-and-methodology comparison that a Europe-centred monitoring process may miss; note the distinct finding on China’s R&D intensity and basic-research allocation under candidate 1.
results.method_and_limitations: R&D PPPs are based on GDP purchasing-power conversion, not R&D-specific prices; the result varies with benchmark year and exchange-rate approach. Input spending is not a direct measure of research quality, frontier capability or technological autonomy. OECD country inputs include self-reported statistics.
results.reviewer_notes: This finding is about scale and the methodological uncertainty of apparent China/US parity, not about Chinese research funding composition (candidate 1). Avoid stating flatly that China overtook the US.

results.verified_title: Ukraine research support evolves from emergency grants toward durable collaboration and research-system rebuilding
results.source_identity_basis: Opened ALLEA’s complete event-report webpage, dated 8 June 2026 and describing the Warsaw General Assembly satellite event and the European Fund for Displaced Scientists. Its exact title and URL match the Strand C source identified in the main Radar manifest.
results.source_type: European academies primary event report / programme monitoring
results.evidence_location: ALLEA 8 June 2026 event report, paragraphs under “From Emergency Support to Ecosystem Building”, “Current Needs and Future Priorities”, and reported EFDS participants/publications. European Commission Ukraine research cooperation overview: “Specific support for Ukrainian research and innovation”.
results.specific_finding: The ALLEA-supported Ukrainian research ecosystem is moving from initial emergency relief toward longer-term institutional rebuilding and cross-border “brain circulation”. ALLEA reports its displaced-scientist fund reached about 140 scholars and contributed to over 300 publications, while independent EU Commission documentation confirms a parallel, larger support architecture including MSCA4Ukraine, EIC4Ukraine and research-infrastructure access.
results.primary_evidence_summary: ALLEA’s June 2026 report explicitly identifies a shift from temporary support to researcher networks, institutional capacities and reintegration pathways. Its EFDS programme figures are programme self-reports, not externally audited impact estimates. European Commission programme documentation independently establishes multiple mechanisms for maintaining Ukrainian research participation and connections during the war.
results.corroboration_assessment: The European Commission describes distinct fellowship, innovation-funding and infrastructure-access schemes, corroborating the broader policy shift toward network and capacity maintenance. It does not independently verify ALLEA’s stated count of 140 scholars or 300 publications, which are therefore clearly attributed to ALLEA.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Researcher mobility and ongoing institutional networks can preserve Ukraine’s scientific capacity under wartime disruption while creating future research cooperation, infrastructure access and reconstruction capabilities. Comparing temporary exile fellowships against sustained collaboration helps evaluate what support actually stabilizes a damaged research system.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The same ALLEA event report already appears as an authoritative Strand C entry in the main Radar. This source-grounded review confirms the subject and extends its interpretation through an independent European Commission programme comparison; it is not a newly discovered item absent from Radar.
results.method_and_limitations: ALLEA’s participant and publication counts are its own outcome claims without independent impact evaluation or a counterfactual; event participants’ assessments cannot establish causal programme effectiveness. Ukraine’s conflict conditions and programme timelines change, and EU cooperation is not the whole Ukrainian research ecosystem.
results.reviewer_notes: Main Radar exact match in Strand C with deep_scan_authoritative=true. Added independent programme context without treating it as proof of EFDS quantitative claims.

results.verified_title: UNESCO Institute for Statistics: 2026 global R&D data release
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the UNESCO Institute for Statistics original news release dated 18 March 2026 (last updated 22 June), which reports global and regional R&D intensity, researcher density, and 43 country-level updates; it does not report US-specific spending or personnel trend figures in the article itself.
results.source_type: UNESCO global statistical release; non-US-specific assigned source
results.evidence_location: UIS 2026 R&D Data Release, Global R&D Investment and Researchers Worldwide sections
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: The UNESCO article establishes global R&D and combined Europe/Northern America regional trends, but the assigned United States slot is not supported by country-specific results on that page. Separate NCSES data verify US federal obligations and potential 2025 declines, yet those are not the same statistic as total US GERD or UIS researcher density. A US-targeted source or explicitly extracted UIS US country series is needed for an evidence-linked KEEP.
results.reviewer_notes: Possible follow-up primary document: US NCSES Survey of Federal Funds for R&D 2024–2025; do not conflate federal agency obligations, total national GERD and researcher FTE.
